analysis.one_liner: Repeals banks' cash and suspicious-transaction reporting and requires warrants for access to financial records.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final weeks of the 117th Congress with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Financial Services Committee and died there when the Congress ended in January 2023, with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would dismantle large parts of the Bank Secrecy Act, the law that requires banks to report cash transactions, suspicious activity, and the real owners of corporate entities to the government so investigators can detect money laundering, tax evasion, and terrorism financing. It would also require the government to get a search warrant before accessing a customer's financial records. It was introduced in October 2022, weeks before the Congress ended, and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and other financial institutions gain the most directly: they would no longer have to file cash transaction reports, suspicious activity reports, or most other reports to government agencies, eliminating a major compliance workload and cost [S2] [S3]. Wealthy individuals and people moving money through shell companies would gain privacy from the financial monitoring regime, since the bill also eliminates reporting on beneficial ownership of corporate entities [S2]. The bill does offer ordinary customers a civil-liberties benefit: government access to financial records would require a search warrant [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the requirements that financial institutions report certain transactions to government agencies for detecting money laundering and terrorism financing, so banks would no longer have to file cash transaction reports or suspicious activity reports [S2].
Eliminates reporting requirements related to the beneficial ownership of corporate entities, so the real owners of companies would no longer have to be identified to the government [S2].

Repeals more than a dozen sections of the Bank Secrecy Act, including currency reporting and foreign transaction provisions, and replaces agency access to financial records with a search warrant requirement under the Right to Financial Privacy Act [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost through weakened enforcement: with banks no longer required to report suspicious transactions or identify corporate owners, investigators would have far less ability to detect money laundering, tax evasion, and terrorism financing [S2]. Law enforcement and financial-crime investigators would lose their main source of leads [S2]. The warrant requirement would also make routine regulatory oversight harder, not just intrusive fishing expeditions.

drawbacks.text: Eliminating banks' transaction reporting would gut the primary tool for detecting illicit activity such as money laundering and terrorism financing [S2].
Removing beneficial ownership reporting would let the owners of corporate entities remain anonymous, making it easier to hide money through shell companies [S2].

Requiring a search warrant for any government access to financial records would go beyond protecting ordinary customers from snooping; it would also block routine regulatory and law-enforcement record requests that currently require far less [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles a real civil-liberties protection (a search warrant before the government pulls your bank records) with a repeal of the reporting regime that financial investigators rely on. The repeal dwarfs the privacy gain: without suspicious-activity and beneficial-ownership reporting, the same institutions and individuals the current law exposes to scrutiny would simply stop being scrutinized, and ordinary people would live with the resulting crime, tax evasion, and terrorism-financing blind spots.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in October 2022 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never held a hearing or markup, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. John W. Rose introduced the bill in the House on October 7, 2022, in the final months of the 117th Congress [S1] [S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services the same day, and no further action was taken [S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died in committee without a hearing, markup, or vote [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Investigators and the public are better off that it died: the bank reporting requirements that flag money laundering, tax evasion, and terrorism financing, and the beneficial ownership rules that identify who is behind a company, remain in force. Banks never received the compliance relief the bill would have handed them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Anti-money-laundering enforcement; banks got no relief

for.name: Rep. John W. Rose
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Financial Services Committee, where it carried no cosponsors.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 7, 2022 and took no further action; no hearing, markup, or vote was scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and never reached a vote, so no partisan division was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would free banks from filing cash-transaction, suspicious-activity, and beneficial-ownership reports, ending a major compliance cost. That relief comes directly at the expense of the transparency regime the public relies on to catch money laundering and tax evasion.

industries.industry: Users of shell companies and offshore finance
industries.note: Eliminating beneficial ownership reporting would keep the real owners of corporate entities anonymous, making it easier to move money without accountability.
The bill strips the reporting pipeline that generates money-laundering and terrorism-financing leads, leaving investigators with warrants as the only route to financial records.
